title: Bouncing ball

slow_motion.evidence: No narration, captions, or visual cues indicate slow motion.

subjects.description: small orange circular ball with white highlight

observation.what_happens: An orange ball travels from the upper left toward the right while falling toward the brown floor, bouncing once and continuing rightward. It is already airborne at the start of the clip and is still in flight when the clip ends.

calibration.note: scale from the fall itself: 356 px/s² over 4 arcs = g of 9.807 m/s²

given: g = 9.807 m/s² (Earth); it set the scale, so treat g as known and fixed
reasoning: x grows almost linearly while y shows repeated fall-and-rise arcs with falling peaks and a common low level near -7.6 m, so a projectile with a restitutive floor hit. Horizontal speed looks nearly constant, but on Earth in air some drag is possible, so vacuum vs linear vs quadratic drag bouncing models compete.

law.title: Gravity plus bouncy floor
law.summary: The ball flies like a textbook projectile and bounces like a bouncy ball.

caveats: Only one bounce was observed, so bounce behavior beyond that is untested.
The ball was already in the air at the start and still flying at the end, so launch and landing are not seen.
critique.finding: The ball falls under gravity {g} and rebounds from the floor {y_floor} keeping {e} of its bounce speed. Adding air drag does not improve the flight.
critique.headline: The ball falls freely; the air barely touches it.
critique.why_it_won: It fits the whole flight with pure gravity and a single bounce, while adding air drag only adds wobble.

headline: The ball falls freely; the air barely touches it.
finding: The ball falls under gravity 9.81 m/s² and rebounds from the floor -7.68 ± 0.0034 m keeping 0.85 ± 1.88e-4 of its bounce speed. Adding air drag does not improve the flight.

eyeball.confidence: low-medium, rough visual estimate from few frames
eyeball.law_in_words: Free-fall under constant g between frames and Newton normal restitution at impact: outgoing vertical speed equals e times incoming vertical speed.
